maintopic: REPORTED INCREASE IN PRICES OF CERTAIN GRADES IN NOVA SCOTLA

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax):	I
should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour, as the minister having jurisdiction over the war-time prices and trade board. Is he aware that while prices of coal from Inverness, Bras d'Or, Indian Cove,
Drummond and other independent mines have not been altered, Halifax prices of all soft coals produced by the Dominion Coal company and subsidiaries have been increased by 25 cents per ton to Halifax consumers? This being so, what action if any does the minister propose to take in the matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: REPORTED INCREASE IN PRICES OF CERTAIN GRADES IN NOVA SCOTLA
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind enough to give me notice of his intention to ask this question, and a few moments ago I obtained the information in connection with it.
I am not in a position to deal with the several mines referred to in his question, the respective coal operators and the variation of prices. But I believe the answer would be this. A little time ago a conciliation board granted wage increases amounting to a very substantial sum to the Dominion Coal company. I believe that now the operators are suggesting a proposal under which there will be some increase in the prices of certain grades of coal. This matter at present is receiving the consideration of the fuel administrator and the war-time prices and trade board, to determine whether such increases are justified.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, March 24, consideration in committee of Bill No. 19, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley^-Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
On section 4-Loans authorized.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the resolution foreshadowing this measure was before the house last month we attempted to amend it so as to secure consideration for a compulsory non-interest-bearing loan, and for the acquisition by the government of the entire banking system of Canada, so that it might become during the war and afterwards an instrument of national policy.

The national ownership and control of the financial system has always been a fundamental policy in our proposals and in our programme. The amendment we made then was ruled out of order, and Mr. Speaker was good enough to indicate that at some future stage such a, resolution might be introduced. This I believe is the stage at which an amendment to the measure is in order. I believe an amendment to this section of the bill would be proper.
To-day we have before us a bill for the raising of $1,300,000,000 for various purposes, and in several ways, in connection with the war. Had we the opportunity now we would move to amend this section to include the acquisition of the chartered banks. But I understand that would not now be in order, because it would involve a further expenditure of public money and, according to the rules, private members may not move for such expenditure.
We must therefore confine ourselves to the amendment of the section to provide that such part of the appropriation as may be raised by way' of loan shall be raised without interest, and levied according to ability to pay.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis):
That paragraph 1 of section 4 be amended by striking out all the words after "raise" in line sixteen, and substituting the following therefor:
"under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, by way of compulsory interest-free loans to be levied according to ability to subscribe, such sum or sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of one billion three hundred million dollars as may be required for the purposes of this act."
and that paragraph 2 of section 4 be amended by the deletion in line twenty-six, of the words "and the interest thereon."
The amended section would then read:
(1)	The governor in council may, in addition to the sums now remaining unborrowed and negotiable of the loans authorized by parliament, by any act heretofore passed, raise under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, by way of compulsory interest-free loans to be levied according to ability to subscribe, such sum or sums of money not exceeding in the whole the sum of one billion three hundred million dollars as may be required for the purposes of this act.
(2)	The principal raised by way of loan under this act shall be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.
This does not of course prevent the government from raising all or a substantial portion of this amount by taxation, or by the use of the Bank of Canada for any direct issue of credit or currency which may at any time at any given moment seem desirable and necessary. Like the original section, it limits

War Appropriation Bill
the amount that may be raised by loan or otherwise to SI,300,000,000. As the minister explained last Thursday at page 1880 of Hansard, the actual amount to be borrowed will be stated when the budget is introduced in the near future.
On the same day the minister expressed himself as being opposed to the principle now included in the proposed amendment. He went farther and said it was not the policy of the government to promote the sale of interest-free bonds on a voluntary basis, as we now have it, by advertising and the like. He made the extraordinary excuse-I thought it was extraordinary-that such a campaign would cause the conscientious, generous and self-sacrificing people to buy the interest-free bonds while the more prudent and selfish would refrain from doing so.
Our amendment meets this very objection, for it would place the prudent and the selfish upon the same basis as the imprudent and the unselfish. Indeed the proposal in our opinion is eminently fair and eminently just. Moreover, what is the object of borrowing money? Is it to finance the war, and for no other purpose? Obviously not, for if we fought wars with money, then the government could issue currency and credit for all our needs. But wars are fought with goods, not with money. It was this truth which Dorothy Thompson had in mind in an article from which I quoted some time ago, and in which she said:
The allies had money, but failed to produce goods. The Germans had no money, but did produce them.
A few days ago I was taken to task by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Ross) for quoting those words with approval. But they are true, and to quote them did not imply approval of the methods Hitler used to regiment and reduce the living standards of the German people, and thus to divert German resources almost exclusively to war production.
Money is not wealth; to think so is a delusion. All wealth is in goods, and no amount of money will suffice if we lack the goods and services which money may buy. This is obvious of course if we consider the position of a beleaguered city. It may have all the credit and all the currency it ever had, but if it lacks the materials of defence, food, munitions and so on, then the accumulation of currency and credit in that beleaguered city will be of no avail.
The real cost of this war must be paid for now in the sacrifice of the things we should like to have, because the raw material, the machines and labour are required for the production of war goods. Therefore to be 14873-116
realistic we must measure the material cost of this war, as of every other war, in things, not in billions of dollars. If we grasp this idea we shall see that no amount of money in our pockets will enable us to buy the luxuries which we must make it impossible to produce. However, in our profit economy the diversion of industry from peace-time requirements to war-time needs is admittedly a most difficult problem. Heavy taxation and the levying of gifts or of loans from large accumulations of wealth must be undertaken. Otherwise, to use the minister's words, the selfish and the prudent will invest their money in the wrong things and industry and labour will be diverted from our war effort, thus defeating the objectives of the conscientious, the generous and the unselfish members of our population.	.
Only to-day I came across an interesting illustration of what I mean. Reference was made recently in the Financial Post to two estates which had recently been probated in the province of Ontario. One estate totalled the enormous sum of $5,229,020. The main item was made up of stock in a mining company, of which the deceased had been the president, amounting to S4,565,000.	Book
debts and promissory notes totalled $540,931; life insurance, $112,182; real estate, $7,590 and personal effects, $3,317. Apparently there had been no subscription to any issue of government bonds. A week or two earlier the same paper published the details of the estate of one of the great industrialists of this same province, a man who had. been the president of one of our great producing corporations. That estate totalled $942,858 made up of stocks in more than thirty companies totalling $670,996; insurance, $166,228; real estate $73,000; cash, $11,965; 'bonds and debentures, $1,467 and other assets, $19,202. The gentleman in question had purchased one $400 war saving certificate and he held one $1,000 five per cent, 1945, Dominion of Canada bond.
I bring these details to the attention of the committee in support of the argument which I am making as well as the argument the minister made for us the other evening. It is contended that any form of loan, whether interest-bearing or non-interest-bearing, merely defers the evil day when the loan will have to be repaid. That is true to a degree. But when we make an appeal in war-time we ask the people in effect, not only to lend money but to forgo the building of new non-essential homes and plants, to defer the purchase of new automobiles or expensive radios, and even to do without some necessities. Our plea is that this should 'be done on a fair and just basis so that the poor, unselfish and sometimes imprudent people will not have to deny

War Appropriation Bill

themselves necessary food. Compulsion should not be exerted only upon the wage earner, the salaried masses and incidentally the farmers whose incomes are to be lowered by restrictions upon the deliveries of grain, tobacco and other produce.
A compulsory non-interest-bearing loan, levied according to ability to pay, is obviously a means of securing something nearer equality of sacrifice. Make those who have a large stake in the outcome of this war because of the wealth [DOT] and property which they control bear their fair share of the burden which the nation is being called upon to carry. There will be some who will say, "Why not a capital levy instead of a non-interest-bearing loan?" To my mind a capital levy should have been made after the last war in order to retire some of the money borrowed on the capital destroyed during the war. Perhaps that is the method we shall have to adopt in part when this war is over in order to retire a substantial portion of the debt we are now assuming.
The proposal which we now make is a constructive suggestion similar to that which was adopted in New Zealand. According to recent articles which appeared in the British press, the same thing is being considered by some people in the United Kingdom. If our war financing is undertaken realistically we shall be able to escape many of the difficulties which caused confusion after the last war. After all, if properly planned and used, the tremendous capital equipment we are now providing for our war effort ought to enrich us when this war ends. It is true that much that we shall have made during the war will be destroyed during its progress or made useless by peace. But we are learning now how to extract from the earth through man's skill and by proper organization much more than we ever extracted before. Thus if we have the sense to profit by this lesson we can enjoy more things than we have ever enjoyed before. In that sense we shall be actually richer as a nation.
War has taught us that the masses do not suffer poverty when there is work to do. It is unemployment which curses many thousands in our midst with poverty. War with its tremendous waste and demands actually ends or at least mitigates unemployment and through the provision of wages and salaries relieves some forms of poverty and distress. This is certainly a paradox, and it is an indictment of our present economic system. It is a problem which we must prepare now to solve when peace comes; for if we do not solve it we shall perish as we deserve to perish. It seems to me that now is the time to consider the

implications of the post-war period. The amendment offers a logical solution to one part of our war financing problem.
We propose that Canada borrow now without interest and on a graduated plan, according to ability to pay, the purchasing power we desire to transfer now from peace to war, and which can and must be transferred again in the future from	war	needs	to	peace-time
requirements. How that transfer shall be made eventually, and upon what kind of basis the loans now being made shall be repaid, the progress of the war and our post-war needs must determine.
One thing is certain. We must not allow this war effort to enrich the so-called prudent and the selfish.	We	must not,	as we aredoing, play into	the	hands	of	those whomonopolize wealth and	power	in this country.
The amendment would do much to prevent us from falling into such a net in the future, and would bring about a measure of that equality of sacrifice of which so much has been said in this house and throughout the country. We ask men to fight; we ask men and women to labour; we ask all to sacrifice. Equally we should ask wealth to place itself now at the disposal of the nation, without interest and without profit. I believe that if something of this sort were done, it would do much to remove from the minds of many of our people the fear that when the war is ended the great masses of the people will not be any better off, indeed will be worse off, and that a few people in the Dominion of Canada will be infinitely richer in accumulated wealth than they were before the war broke out.
In my opinion we have not yet been able to obtain that enthusiasm for the cause in which we are involved that we ought to have obtained. If this is a war, as I believe it is, for the preservation of our democratic way of life, then it seems to me that the nation has the right to ask those who, through fortuitous circumstances as well as by their own endeavours, have been able to accumulate this nation's goods, to lend their wealth freely to the nation. I am not even suggesting that we ask them at this moment to give it, though later we may have to ask them to give some of their wealth. But certainly at this time we have a right to ask them to lend to this nation in her hour of need their wealth without interest and without profit. I am urging the government to accept this point of view and to allow this clause to be amended in order that the portion of this appropriation which is to be raised by loan may be raised by a graduated loan based on ability to

War Appropriation Bill
subscribe, and that the money shall be loaned without interest at least for the duration of the war.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question before he resumes his seat?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. member said to-day what he said when making a similar amendment some weeks ago, that the particular form of loan he proposes was adopted in New Zealand. My reading, which might not be complete, is to the effect that while New Zealand has passed general legislation which would permit the government to levy an enforced loan, interest-free, in the same manner as our mobilization act permits this government to do many things which have not yet been done, New Zealand as a matter of fact has not yet taken action in the matter of interest-free enforced loans. Would the hon. member tell the committee what action, if any, New Zealand has taken in that matter? I am asking for information.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In the summer, I think it was, or in the fall, I quoted from the budget speech of the Minister of Finance of the Dominion of New Zealand, who made the definite statement that money would be raised in New Zealand this fiscal year by means of a non-interest-bearing loan. I have before me the Montreal Standard of March 8, 1941, which contains an article headed "New Zealanders Taxed for Social Experiments and on Top of That, War," in the course of which it is stated:
The government (of New Zealand) expects to realize an additional $26,000,000 from 15,000 individuals and 3,000 corporate taxpayers through a compulsory war loan on which no interest will be paid for three years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What was the amount?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The amount stated in the Montreal Standard is $26,000,000. That sum does not quite agree with my recollection of the statement made by the Minister of Finance of New Zealand when he introduced his budget last June. As I recollect it, he stated then that New Zealand expected to raise in the neighbourhood of fifteen million pounds, which would be closer to $60,000,000, at current rates of exchange, than the sum mentioned in the Montreal Standard. I think it is clear, both from his budget speech and from the paragraph I have just quoted, that such a loan has actually been raised in the Dominion of New Zealand.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Before this amendment is voted upon I wish to make a remark or two. The last time the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) brought this amendment forward the Social Credit group supported it as the lesser of two evils. The present system of debt and taxation is a very grievous evil. Taxation, if it is persevered in as this government seems determined to persevere in it, will ultimately destroy the standards of living of the people of Canada. First it will decrease the production of the Canadian productive machine because it will heighten the cost of production; second, it will ultimately deplete the resources with which producers must produce, and, third, it will bring about a failing of markets both at home and abroad.
Furthermore, this system will develop grave dangers of inflation through irregularity of production. As matters now stand there is no way in which the governing power in Canada appears to be able to cause the kind of production it wants or to prevent or divert the very kind of production it does not want. The result is that we might have a dangerous scarcity of certain commodities in this country and a dangerous superabundance of other commodities. This is one of -the conditions which will bring about inflation.
Let us bear in mind that inflation is a rise in prices which results from a shortage of goods. The policy which is being followed to-day of a general, blanket taxation as heavy as the people can possibly stand is aggravating the tendencies to inequality and irregularity and unbalance of production, and will continue to do so more and more. There is altogether too little appreciation of just w-h-at inflation is and what causes it and -how it is to be overcome. As soon as there is a complete understanding of the matter on all sides, there will be no doubt of -the accuracy of the remark which I have just made, that the present system of debt and taxation is leading to inflation.
Furthermore, the system which is now being followed may ultimately impair Canada's credit-perhaps irrecoverably. It is one thing to make wise-cracks about certain governments that have declared themselves unable to meet their commitments with respect to debt; it is entirely another thing to face facts and to realize that the government at Ottawa, if it continues to plunge this country headlong into debt, will ultimately arrive at the point at which it will no longer be able to meet its commitments and to maintain its rate of interest.
These points which I have mentioned indicate the inevitable tendency and danger and result

War Appropriation Bill
of borrowing and taxation. Altogether the polity is a dangerous one. There are so many who seem to assume that the way we are proceeding now is the sound way. There was a time when farmers believed that the only sound way of travelling was by horse and buggy or horse and wagon, and that the only sound way of harvesting their crops was with a sickle and by means of hand binding. Today everyone -has outgrown such antiquated notions. The very devices which used to be sound came, as a result of the development of certain forces in the world, to be unsound. The financial system which we have traditionally followed is becoming unsound because of the development of great forces on the earth.
I have said this much to indicate that the present system is a great danger. We thought as a Social Credit group that for the time being it was safer to cause people to subscribe to interest-free loans than it was to go forward indefinitely with the present system of borrowing and taxation.
But times have changed. Forced loans, which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has advocated in his amendment, are a danger. It matters not whether New Zealand or any other country in the world has resorted to them; they are a danger. They would be more subversive of Canada's economic wellbeing than even the system which is now being followed.
In the first place, the surpluses of money which had accumulated and which were to be found when the amendment was last presented have now, I believe, been largely dissipated as a result of rigid taxation and aggressive government borrowing. In my opinion, what surpluses now remain are needed for productive enterprise in this country. Forced loans tend to discourage people. I find in my contacts with men and women from day to day that there is developing in Canada a very unfortunate attitude of pessimism and uncertainty and anxiety and discouragement, because people feel that there is simply no use in striving. This is the logical result of the taxation we now are using. It will be, more still, the result of forced loans.

seem to fight very hard for very little.

We will grant that
the soldiers fight very hard for very little. But I do not think you will find farmers doing that, although they are loyal enough; I do not think you will find mine owners, oil producers, munition makers or clothing manufacturers spending their hours for nothing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mine owners don't work!

Mine owners

They had
better take over the coal mines, then.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is another
aspect of the forced loan to which I object. It is a step towards communism. I was a bit disgusted last evening, while the hon. member for North Battleford was giving what I regarded as a very fine speech, to hear four or five hon. members across the way come out with the word "communism." I wonder whether such people know what communism is.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is communism?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am not sure that
I know; but this, I believe, is one of the concepts of it: that it stands for taking away from people what they have; it is based on state ownership. Now, if the state takes away from people the money they have toiled to earn and save, surely the state is making a step towards communism, unless I am entirely misinformed as to what communism is. In other words, we have just been hearing reasons advanced for a step towards communism; and no one used the word "communism" when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was speaking! Yet when the hon. member for North Battleford was advocating better schools and further health measures and more of many things which every hon. member knows we ought to have, certain people were foolhardy enough to whisper "communism." I must say, Mr. Chairman, attitudes like that utterly confound me.
This really is a step towards communism. Whether the government or the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar wishes to introduce communism, it is certainly, in my opinion, a move in that direction.
Moreover, it is a step towards totalitarianism, towards regimentation, towards cen-

War Appropriation Bill
tralization. Totalitarianism, regimentation, centralization are characteristics of the very foe we fight.
But, people will say, what are you going to do? Well, Mr. Chairman, that is just the question we should have begun to ask ourselves two years ago. If the system which we are using to-day is such that we face an inevitable break-down, as a result of which we are first advised and then urged to adopt measures which we all abhor, it should be evident that the system we are endeavouring to apply is at bottom fallacious, unsound.
The proposal for forced loans is a step towards reducing all to poverty instead of raising the people to prosperity. There seems to be an idea on the part of some people that some people are poor because other people are rich. I have never been impressed by the reasoning of those who hold so. We could take all the money and possessions away from the few who possess them and distribute them evenly among all the population and still have everybody poor. The solution certainly does not lie along that path, the path of reducing everybody to poverty. The solution lies in the direction of raising everybody to prosperity; and in a country like Canada that is unquestionably possible. Those who maintain that it is not possible have simply not thought far enough through the problem.
It is plain common sense that in a country like Canada, with such an abundance of resources, a country so varied, with such people as we have in Canada, with such industrial equipment, means of transportation and organization generally, there can certainly be prosperity for everyone even while we fight the most terrible war the world has ever seen. If the system we are following to-day denies this fact, then the system condemns itself.
The present proposal is only one of the devices which will be urged upon the governments of our land under the present system. If we continue making attempts to do the impossible, such as making an antiquated financial system work in a modern age to fight a modern war, a forced loan is simply one of the desperate expedients and doubtful experiments to which governments will be tempted to resort more and more as the days go by.
Some people will ask, "Well, what is your solution?" I have no intention of offering a solution; I am merely explaining the reasons why my group are not going to support the amendment. I will say though, in passing and in closing, that the solution lies along
the line of wisely using our national credit.
Such a use will -obviate the need of, and the urge towards, such extreme measures as this one.
To those who feel disposed to smile, let me put this question baldly: Is it not common sense that a country as wealthy as Canada is in resources should be able to fight this war and still have prosperity? Everyone will say, "Yes." Next, can the system we are following enable us to do that? Everyone will say, "No." Very well, then; there must be a way out. Now, where is the way out? If we set to work as members to find the way out we shall begin to do some effective thinking; -we shall begin to do the things we came here to do.
I am going to move an amendment to the amendment as follows:
That the amendment be amended by striking out all the words after "therefor" in the third line thereof, and substituting the following:
Under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. 1931, by way of interest-free money obtained from the Bank of Canada, such sum or sums of money not exceeding in the whole the sum of one billion three hundred million dollars as may be required for the purpose of this act. Before the minister speaks. I wish to direct the attention of the committee to citations 551 and 552 in Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms. Section 4 of the bill which is now under consideration is submitted by the government, and the proposal is to raise the amount necessary to carry out the provisions of the act by way of an interest-bearing loan. The amendment proposes to raise that money by way of a compulsory interest-free loan to be levied according to the ability to subscribe such sum or sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of $1,300,000,000, as may be required for the purpose of the act. I quote:
551.	It is a fundamental principle that no resolution or amendment to increase a charge upon the people can be moved with the Speaker in the chair; it must be initiated in committee by a minister acting on behalf of the crown.
No. 552 reads:
552.	Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, example of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals. Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee: but these
War Appropriation Bill

proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year. Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as, for instance, a proposal to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property as an alternative for an inhabited house duty, the necessity of new taxation, to that extent, being .already declared on behalf of the crown.
In my opinion the proposed amendment increases the burden upon the people and it does not lie -within the power of a private member to move such an amendment in committee. It should be moved by a minister acting on behalf of the crown.

speechtext:
Before this section carries I should like to say a word or two on the subject of information. I had hoped to be able to make these remarks yesterday but the minister of information was away on business, so I should like to avail myself of his presence here to-day to say just a word or two on this subject.
There is no need to emphasize to this house or any other body the importance of information during this war; it cannot be exaggerated. All I wish to do is urge upon the government that the very excellent work described in the minister's statement of March 7 should be carried on and extended with all the pressure and urgency that the minister, with his very great ability, can bring to bear. Obviously, early in the war this government decided that it would not be proper for it to issue propaganda in the United States. With that decision I think every hon. member of this house was thoroughly in accord; and when friends in the United States asked me why we Canadians were not telling about the things we were doing in the war I always answered by saying, "Is it not much better that we should

say too little than that we should say too much?" I think everyone who has thought about the matter was in thorough agreement with that policy, but we see where it brought us on several occasions. Representative Maas and Senator Nye, two of the leading isolationists in the United States, urged upon the United States congress and senate that Canada was not playing its part in the war, that we were not matching the United States lease-lend effort. In the United States our war effort was not thoroughly appreciated, and we did not have the flow of tourists backward and forward through which we might carry on those normal, friendly contacts we have always had with our neighbours to the south. In the New York Times of yesterday Mr. P. J. Phillips says that Canada's ban on publicity in the United States is to be lifted. I certainly hope that we are going to give more information in the United States, for a good many reasons which must be obvious to all. If we are to continue to have the close, friendly relations with the United States that we always have had and should always have, the United States must understand what we are doing, and we must express ourselves, our aims and our actions, to the people of that country.
This week, Mr. Chairman, there is an added reason for taking this matter more seriously. The London Economist in its current issue is reported to state that we in Canada should have a lease-lend bill like that of the United States. There again what we are doing is not properly understood, and with all respect I suggest to the minister that here is another opportunity for his department and the other branches of the government to increase the work they are doing abroad.
I suggest also that there is room for an intensification of information service at home. The fact that this debate has gone on for twenty-one days indicates that there is a lack of appreciation of what is being done. Had even more information been given, it is possible that the debate would not have lasted as long as it has. But I suggest that the way to give information, in addition to giving it here in the house, is through the press releases issued by the government in the ordinary course.
Within the last few days I had the very great privilege of visiting Halifax harbour and Sussex camp, and of seeing aeroplane factories and munitions works. I was immensely impressed with what I saw and with the appearance of the alert, fit men who are doing our jobs for us in those places. I suggest that if all the members of this committee had seen what there is to be seen of our war work in the various camps, ports and munitions works, a great deal of the

War Appropriation Bill
criticism that has been expressed here during the last few weeks never would have been uttered at all. There I saw men from all parts of Canada, men of whom any part of Canada might be proud. We cannot bring all the people to the Halifax and Sussex camps, but we can bring Halifax harbour and the Sussex camp to the people by means of the movies and broadcasting and the publications of the department of information. This department has been doing most useful work. The films that have been prepared are magnificent, but I think more can be done to bring home to the people of Canada a realization of the wonderful work that is being done and that is too often deprecated here and elsewhere.
It is exceedingly difficult in Canada to translate this figure of $1,300,000,000 into munitions, planes, tanks and trained men and women working eight-hour shifts, day and night, turning out things necessary for our security. Unless this can be visualized by the people and by this house, then it is apt to be felt that this sum represents just so much money or so much talk. What a story there is to tell! It is a story of which every Canadian should be proud. During the last eighteen months we have multiplied our air force tenfold, our army fortyfold and our navy tenfold. Each day we are raising and spending $2,700,000, while in the last war the figure was only $117,000. The expenditures for which we are providing in this appropriation, together with the amounts required for the repatriation of securities, are five times the expenditures during the corresponding period of the last war, and more than the entire cost of the last war. That is the picture the people need to see. That is why I say this figure must be translated into things they can see and words they can understand. That is the job the department of information has been doing, the job that I hope it will do more thoroughly as time goes on.
These are difficult times, Mr. Chairman. We are at perhaps the most serious stage of the war. These are times that try men's souls. We need, and the government need, all the support and help they can get from every source, and I suggest that the department of information has a task to perform in telling the story so that the government may get that support. The exploits of our men in the air, the indomitable courage of our merchant marine, the endurance of the people of England have won the admiration of the world and have called forth our gratitude day by day. In the air, on land and at sea the heroic age has returned to our race, and that is the story that should be told.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The country has taken this huge expenditure with a great deal of good grace. But the business men of Canada do not wish to permit the functions of the House of Commons to be usurped by scores of orders in council. We have seen the effect of orders in council in connection with what has happened concerning the National Resources Mobilization Act. This huge war expenditure is what we are getting because over a period of twenty years parliament had become so strongly Geneva-minded.
In my opinion this section is unnecessary. Parliament meets from time to time, and there is no necessity to give the governor in council such vast, wide powers-powers which practically override the financial structure of Canada. They override our tariff provisions- and all this is done merely by order in council. It has the effect of adding further burden to the hard-pressed industries and businesses of Canada.
The artificial burdens, barriers and restraints of trade to which business men are subjected render it almost impossible for them to conduct their business. This bill smacks of the Marxian policy of the totalitarian states. It may also be a gesture to hon. members to my left. It may be the intention to give them a loaf in this way, and to decline to give it to them in the manner that has been described this afternoon.
If Hitler comes he will care nothing about our financial structure. He will not consider whether we have a government composed of Liberals, Conservatives, Social Crediters or members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. Before this measure passes the government should tell the country to what extent its financial programme to be carried out by order in council will interfere with the normal peace-time 'business of the wholesalers, retailers and grocers. In my opinion the aim should be to add to the production of armaments without a shortage of non-defence consumption, and without unnecessary substitution of goods used in every day consumption.
As I said the other day this country' has unlimited resources. Our natural resources from coast to coast are vast. We have financial resources and, notwithstanding the measures brought down by the government in connection with war expenditures, I say we have a reserve of labour. There is still a large reserve force of labour, and especially of people over forty-five years of age. Those are men with technical experience, and well able to help.
The people of Canada are behind the war effort to the utmost extent, but I must object to giving the government of the day the vast liberties set out in this measure. In our experience in connection with the National
War Appropriation Bill

Resources Mobilization Act, we see what happens when we give power to act by order in council. We gave the government supreme power over the liberty of the subject, and over all other statutes which safeguarded our liberties.
What has happened in connection with conscientious objectors? With its power to pass orders in council, *what did the government do? Instead of giving those people work in military districts, or sending them to Iceland or to Greenland's icy mountains, by the time the government has finished I am convinced it will wind up, by order in council, by presenting every conscientious objector in Canada with a gold watch and an illuminated address. That is what happens when we have government by order in council.
Has the business community been consulted about this section? Have officials of the Bank of Canada been consulted? Have the so-called brain trusts, which appear to be doing very little at the present time, been consulted? Does the manner of proceeding under section 5 fit into the lease-lend bill? Does this section take into account the effect it will have on that bill? How will it affect the negotiations now pending with Washington concerning parity of the dollar? The United States has made some arrangements with other north American countries, and in my opinion there should be some explanation of the very wide powers conferred under this section. If we are to pass legislation of this kind, we might as well abolish any further control over the financial structure of the country.

Prescribe administrative practices with respect to contracts and agreements for the execution of any public work or for the acquisition of lands-
And so on. If a munitions plant is to be erected on land expropriated by authority of an order in council, has the expropriating authority the right to pay the owner of the land anything it desires to pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
This subsection has for its purpose the strengthening of the cabinet's control over departments. For example it might be felt desirable to lift war transactions out of the scope of the Public Works Act or the Department of Transport Stores Act. Likewise the desire might be to have a uniform practice with respect to purchases. At the present time a department, except that of Munitions and Supply, goes to council for a woi-ks contract involving $5,000, but it can buy S50.000 or more of equipment without coming for an order in council. Generally 
speaking the intent is to provide the necessary power to the governor in council to make such rules as are considered necessary. It also permits pool orders for materials and supplies. It gives the governor in council wide powers with regard to the acquisition of lands. I do not think that in the acquisition of lands the governor in council would be bound by the provisions of other acts, once this act is passed. That is the object of the measure.
This subsection was contained in a similar section of the last appropriation bill. The whole of section 5 is identical with that of section 5 in the 1940 act.

speechtext: Perhaps the question I have in mind has no connection whatsoever with this paragraph. I have in mind a resident in my constituency who about twenty years ago purchased land in a subdivision which had been opened up outside the city of Welland. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Some complaints were made to me in connection with the taking over of land at Tracadie in the county of Gloucester for the new artillery range. After investigation and having the facts supported by affidavits I came to the conclusion that generally speaking the prices offered were fair and reasonable. I happened to know the right of way agent who was acquiring the land for the government and he promised to review all cases that I named. There were instances where there was a difference of opinion or perhaps a difference of judgment as to the value of the land. My own view is that the government was endeavouring to pay a fair price, not the large price that some people would like to get from the government in war time. In this case I think the land is being acquired by the Department of National Defence, but I want to say that I believe they are trying to protect the public treasury. After I had investigated a series of cases where exception was taken to the amount offered, they promised to review them. Perhaps the method followed was a little harsh. I understand that these people were told that if they did not take what was offered, the government would expropriate the land and if they did not get a court decision for more than had been offered they would have to pay all costs. Perhaps that was turning on the heat a little too much, but on the whole I think the job has been done in a decent way. This is certainly not carping criticism.

Many hundreds of millions of dollars have been advanced to companies to do war work. This money has been advanced in various ways. In some cases the government have built buildings, in other cases they have purchased machinery and in other cases the companies have bought machinery on government account. What is going to happen to this machinery after the war is over? I suggest that a permanent commission be set up so that proper records can be kept and a study made of what will be done with this machinery and these plants after the war. Now is the time to tackle this problem. We should not wait until the war is over.
When the Minister of Munitions and Supply went to England the men in the aeroplane industry were rather pleased because they thought that he would discuss matters with the British people and they would know when he returned just what was going to be done. But so far no policy for the future has been laid down, and no announcement has been made by the government as to what planes are going to be ordered or what planes will be required. Some of the men in the aeroplane industry are beginning to get to the end of their tether as far as work is concerned. Unless some policy is announced and orders given out they will not know where they are. In some factories men have been laid off. I just bring this matter to the attention of the government. For the sake of the industry I think some statement of policy should be made by the government.

group rather than another, but since I have been in the Department of Finance I have never seen any real ground for an accusation against one income group rather than another. While I am on my feet may I ask why no consideration has been given to the plight of the potato farmers in Prince Edward Island
War Appropriation Bill

and New Brunswick? Potatoes are selling in Prince Edward Island at 24 cents a bushel, or 60 cents a barrel, without any appreciable market. The farmers of eastern Canada who grow potatoes as their principal crop are just at the end of their tether. They have had ten years of this sort of thing, with one on two exceptional seasons in between. They have used up their reserves and their resources. In addition, the price of their fertilizer has steadily increased, largely as a result of the legislation passed by this government in the baby budget last fall; the cost of exchange was increased, and the ingredients of the fertilizer have to be imported. The potato farmers see their neighbours in the Annapolis valley being bonused. They see that our friends the wheat farmers of the west have at least had their prices stabilized, no matter what the opinion may be as to the adequacy of the price to be received by them. Over and above that they observe this gesture on the part of the government, that men shall be bonused for non-producing. But not one word from this government with respect to the farmers of the maritime provinces, aside from the apple growers. If the government can provide a war appropriation of $6,600,000 to dispose of unmarketable agricultural surpluses, they can do something for the potato farmers of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
I do not understand why these people are forgotten. The industry is an important one in the northern part of the Saint John river valley. I have often urged that these men get back into other varieties of production. They look across to the county of Aroostook in the state of Maine and they see that the potato men there make a strike one year in three or four. There is no doubt about it that occasionally over there they make a real strike. But it is a crop for which the soil of our growers is adapted. They have the machinery, they are able to produce, and they do not lightly yield their desire to do their own planning. I am more particularly interested in the growere of New Brunswick because I know their situation a little better. I have lived among them, gone around among them, and tried to assist them as an individual and in every way I could. I have put money in those farms, a good deal of which I shall never get back, nor do I expect to get it back. But they have a right to ask this government, when it has adopted the policy as a war measure of asking the general taxpayers of the country to put up $6,600,000 for surplus agricultural products, that it should give them at least some consideration. position is not good enough for the potato farmers of New Brunswick. They want to know why they have been overlooked.

I should like to make a few observations on this section, which provides:
Upon the governor in council making an allotment of any part of the one billion three hundred million dollars ($1,300,000,000) granted by this act to provide for the cost of any service, the Minister of Finance shall cause an accounting record to be maintained in a form that will disclose the financial commitments entered into and the expenditure made as a consequence of the allotment being provided for the service concerned.
Predicated on that, there will always be available to the government, and should be available to the country at stated intervals, statements of the expenditures as made under the authority of this section, and in a form that will disclose exactly what expenditures have been made in consequence of the allotment. I have not looked up the record, but I think last year I appealed to the Minister of Finance to lay before parliament within a limited period-I am not sure whether or not it was after the end of the fiscal year-a statement of this accounting of expenditures. I suggest to him that that is a reasonable request, and that if we had had something like that before us during the last three or four weeks, we would have made much more rapid progress than we did make. Instead of a procedure of hit or miss, catch as catch can, as we know was the situation in connection with discussions in committee, we would have had by operation of law and by direction of the house a statement placed before us in convenient form before we began to discuss the appropriation for the coming year, upon which matter we have spent so much time.
I appeal to the minister, as I believe I appealed to him on a former occasion, to amend this section by providing that there shall be laid before parliament a statement of the expenditures based upon section 6. That is what ought to happen and what the trustees ought to be obliged to do. It seems to me
War Appropriation Bill

that that would bring about a great saving of time in the discussion of war appropriation bills. If we had had that a month ago, this bill would have long since been passed, and we would have had much more information than we have received up to the present time.
Why, Mr. Chairman, we have just touched the fringe of the expenditure of 8700,000,000 for last year and the proposed $1,300,000,000 for this year I In a great body of 245 members I doubt if it is possible to do a thorough job in the examination of expenditures made under last year's bill. This body is too large and too unwieldy. We have, as I say, only touched the fringe of the proposed expenditure of $1,300,000,000 to be made in the coming fiscal year.
I am not going to take any blame or responsibility for the delay in the discussion. That blame is on the administration because of its not having given us in the early stages of the discussions in committee a succinct break-down of the money which parliament voted so willingly in the months of June and July last. I suggest that in the interests of the orderly conduct of the business of the House of Commons it should be made incumbent upon the Department of Finance at the next session as early as possible to submit to the house at least an interim statement of the expenditures, we will say, between the 1st of April and the succeeding six months, at which time probably parliament will not be in session.
I offer this suggestion in the spirit of goodwill. Before the bill has received third reading, I hope the minister will give consideration to what I believe is a constructive suggestion and one which in the end will save parliament a great deal of time and money.

But I do not think the annual report of the auditor general is satisfactory for this purpose. It may be that we are wedded to an old system, and that we do not like to depart from it. Probably if we have to, we will get used to a new set-up. But the present condition is not satisfactory. The report comes to us too late to be of any use in discussing current events or current expenditures.
I did submit this to the minister in the utmost of good faith, and he has rebuffed me. I do not know what more I can do. I suggest to the Prime Minister-and I now make my appeal to him

that he give consideration to what I considered last session and what I now consider to be a reasonable request on behalf of the people of Canada, who are paying this money, so that their representatives in parliament may know at the earliest possible moment what is being done with their money.
On many occasions I have said in the house that the people of Canada will give this government, or any government charged with the responsibility of our war effort, all the money required to carry on that war effort. I have no doubt as to the truth of that statement. But per contra they will demand at the earliest possible moment a just and true accounting of how those moneys have been expended. If we abdicate that function in Canada and in the House of Commons, then I suggest we are not performing our proper functions as representatives of the people.

Interim Supply
It is true that under the War Measures Act we are being governed by order in council, and that parliament has been reduced to the status of a body which passes votes of money and which hands over blank cheques to the government to be filled in, in the manner they see fit. That is more or less inevitable in war time; I do not think it could be done in any other way. But the corollary is true, that because confidence is placed in the administration, that administration should rise to the occasion and submit to the people a full accounting of how the money has been spent. Surely that is a reasonable proposition.
If the right hon. gentleman were sitting here and that principle were promoted, I am sure he would get in behind the demand for its support. I well remember his attitude and that of his colleagues in days gone by in connection with votes for relief-and quite properly so. This is war time, and necessities for greater expenditures, rapid expenditures, speedy expenditures are constantly arising. All I am contending for is the principle of trusteeship. This government, the trustees of the people, should render an accounting unto Caesar-and the people are Caesar.

On February 18 I introduced the war appropriation bill now under discussion. I stated that 8700,000,000 had been supplied last spring for the current fiscal year. I pointed out that up to January 31, 1941, approximately $538,000,000 of that sum had been expended. I broke that amount down into the amounts spent on militia services, naval services, and on the air force. Further, I gave a sub-breakdown for the amount allocated to the air force. I pointed out the amount spent on other defence services, in the Department of Munitions and Supply and in other departments. That break-down is to be found in Hansard for February 18, 1941, page 822. That was the day after the house reassembled.
The information I placed on record at that time was as to the amount which had been expended, and the purposes for which the expenditures had been made. I expected that if any further break-down were required, it would be asked for. Later, in the month of March, that further break-down was asked for, and I gave it. Hansard for March 10, page 1363, shows a further break-down of the $538,000,000. It was slightly inaccurate, because the amount was $536,000,000. I explained at every stage that there might be slight inaccuracies, but I offered at all times to give information if it was required. There has been the fullest accounting and the promptest conveying of information to the hon. gentleman and to other members of the house.
When the hon. gentleman says that information has been dragged out of us, that we have given information reluctantly and only when we were forced to, he is making a misrepresentation of the facts. We have given a strict accounting and have offered to give further information at every stage. We are prepared to do so again. We do not wish the impression to go out to the country or to members of this house that we have not been giving information just as soon as it was asked for and just as fully as it was possible to give it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I had intended making a few remarks when the amendment was moved in committee, but the ruling of the chair made that impossible. However, before submitting the reasons why in my opinion this amendment should be accepted by the house, may I make it clear that in proposing the amendment we are not opposing the appropriation. We merely propose an alternative way by which the money may be raised, or at least that part of it which will be raised by way of loan.
I believe the house is unanimously of opinion that the appropriation should be passed-and more, as occasion demands. We are unanimous in that regard because we all realize that we are fighting nations which have glorified war and which have made deceit, force, fear and terror the methods by which they negotiate with other countries.

speechtext: Plus brutality.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes. There can be no peace for us or for the world until victory shall crown the efforts of those who desire that the democratic way of life and the rule of law shall prevail. I am satisfied that all hon. members in this group agree wholeheartedly with the sentiments I have just expressed. If there is any difference of opinion in the house, it is as to the most socially desirable method of financing our war effort. There are at least two definite reasons why our method of floating war loans should be accepted. First, it is the psychologically desirable method; second, it is the method economically desirable. I shall take only a few moments to support those two reasons.
It is psychologically desirable because, whether we like it or not, or whether we accept it or not, we are living in a class society, and there is a strong feeling in large sections of the country that only one class is being asked to-day to do the sacrificing. In other words, acceptance of the method we propose would go a long way toward bringing about equality of sacrifice. It may be answered that we have that now, that we are all making sacrifices, and that we are all in the front line. In the language of the street, I would say that that is all hooey. In Canada we have not even begun to make sacrifices- that is, except a very small fraction of the population. So far the only people who have made sacrifices are, first, the men who have enlisted and put their lives at the disposal of the country and, second, those who are in receipt of very small incomes and find their standard of living being lowered because of the increase in prices which has already taken place. These people with small incomes have a hard time to get along, but they are anxious

War Appropriation-Mr. Maelnnis
to do whatever they can. But they see other people going on as before just as though we were not engaged in a life-and-death struggle.
Let me give two or three examples of what I have in mind. I gave one example to the house some days ago. A woman in Regina in receipt of an income of $20 a month agreed to buy one war savings certificate a month. She pointed out to the young woman who solicited her subscription that to buy the certificate she would have to forgo one meal a day. The Montreal Gazette, that strong champion of things as they are, referred to this as a gracious gesture.
I should like to give another illustration, and if the old lady's act was a gracious one, this one is disgraceful. A few days ago some one sent me a page from the Vancouver Sun containing an architect's drawing of a beautiful home being built for a man in Vancouver, at an estimated cost of $100,000. It is to be 150 feet long and thirty or forty feet wide and will contain fifteen bedrooms; the basement is to contain a number of rooms for entertainment. There will be a room for moving pictures as well as rooms for other kinds of games. If the sacrifice made by the old lady in Regina was a gracious one, the lack of sacrifice on the part of the man building this home is a disgraceful example at a time when we are all said to be in the front line. In order that things like this may not continue, we suggest that people who can afford to build $100,000 homes should be compelled to subscribe to non-interest bearing war bonds.
I noticed the other day that Doctor Staple-ford, director of voluntary services in the Department of National War Services, was advising Canadians to be patriotic, to be proud to wear an old suit of clothes or to drive an old car. If it is patriotic to wear an old suit of clothes, then I have about the most patriotic people in Canada in my constituency. They nearly all wear old clothes because they cannot buy new ones, and most of them cannot afford to buy even an old car. The same can be said of the great majority of people in all constituencies. This is another reason why we should compel people to subscribe to the financing of the war effort according to their ability.
Last month we concluded a drive to get people to subscribe to war savings certificates. I noticed that as soon as the campaign was over, the chairman went on a vacation to the Bahamas or Bermuda in order to get over the effects of his strenuous work. But hundreds of thousands of those who subscribed for war savings certificates have to count every solitary cent. As an unemployed man in the old country said to a government agent some TMr. Maclnnis.]
time ago, even a pair of shoe-laces is important to an unemployed man. He said he had strings in his shoes instead of laces. We must remember that almost every man, woman or child beyond a certain age is able to read, and they know what is going on. They have nearly all the sources of information that those in authority have. They cannot be fooled any longer that there is equality of sacrifice when in fact there is no equality of sacrifice.
I have in my hand a compilation of the debt of Canada which was prepared by the former member for Huron North, Mr. Deach-man, who I understand is now director of publicity for the Department of Munitions and Supply. I should like to draw these figures to the attention of the house in order that hon. members may understand what we have in mind when we advocate the issuing of interest-free bonds. Mr. Deachman showed that the direct expenditures of the last war were $1,698,619,000. Since the war the cost of pensions has amounted to $770,563,000. The cost of soldiers' civil reestablishment has been $258,750,000. The cost of maintaining war graves has been $4,811,000. The cost of administration of soldiers' settlement has been $28,055,000 and the estimated loss on this work is $100,000,000. He then shows that the amount paid in interest from 1915, or when the bonds were first floated, to the end of 1938, was $2,153,465,000, and we still have the principal of $1,698,619,000 to pay.
I receive dozens of letters from widows of veterans complaining that their pensions were stopped when their husbands died. Here is the situation. A man enlisted in the last war and served overseas for whatever time was necessary. He may have been wounded or his health may have been impaired so that on discharge he was granted a pension. He dies, and the pension stops.
Another man stayed at home. He bought Victory bonds and drew the interest on them from the day he bought them until he died, and after he had passed away the interest on the bonds continued to be paid to his widow. Surely, when we are asking people to give their lives in this war, is it too much to ask people to give their money?
The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) in his address this afternoon said that we would be taking this money away from people. Not at all. We are asking people to lend their money to the country because the country needs it; and when the war is over, if we are in a position to pay the principal back-and this applies, of course, whether the loan is with interest or without-the lender will be repaid what he loaned, without interest.

War Appropriation-Mr. Maclnnis
We are not taking anything away from him. All we ask is that every one of us should be willing to give what we have in order that we may help to win this war. We should be willing to do that or we are not sincere when we say that we want to win the war.
The hon. member for Lethbridge this afternoon made a number of observations that seemed curious to me. For example, he called this kind of compulsory loan more subversive than the ordinary way of raising money. I do not believe that even the present way of raising money: loans with interest is subversive. I am, however, quite satisfied that there is nothing subversive about a compulsory non-interestbearing loan. He went on to say he was of opinion that already the surplus accumulations of money in this country had been absorbed by taxation and through the war loans already floated. The hon. gentleman is not watching the accumulations of money as closely as he should be, because the returns made by the chartered banks show that on December 31, 1940, savings deposits in the chartered banks amounted to $1,641,000,000 in round figures. One month later, by January 31, savings deposits had increased to $1,668,000,000, or an increase of over $27,000,000 in savings deposits in one month. It seems to me that there is no excuse for an hon. member not knowing these facts.
As I pointed out when the resolution on which this bill is based was under discussion, war economy changes the normal situation. While in ordinary peace time, at any time between, say 1929 and 1939, it might have been desirable to have an issue of money, it is not desirable at the present time, and we might as well get that fact clear in our minds. The more we get our war industries into production, the greater the number of people who go into war industries, and the greater the number of men who join the armed forces, the more imperative it will be for us to increase our taxation enormously or to raise large sums of money by borrowing. An hon. member beside me asks me to explain why. The reason is that by the production of war supplies we are putting purchasing power into circulation, and we are also putting money into circulation for the ordinary consumers' goods, but only the consumers' goods appear on the market. The war supplies are taken by the government and they do not appear on the market in the ordinary way. Consequently, the more war production we have, the greater the competition there will be for the more limited amount of the ordinary consumable goods on the market, and prices will therefore rise.
Whether we like it or not, there is no way of dealing with that situation except by taxation at a terrific rate-and remember that taxation at the necessary rate would be confiscation-or by borrowing. We are asking that the borrowing be without interest so that when this war is over, we shall not have to pay over the next twenty-five years more in interest than the principal amounted to in the first place, and then have the principal to pay. In twenty years at five per cent each year we can pay off the whole of any loan, but we can never pay off the debts contracted in this war if we follow the old method. I believe it would be not only more sound economically but also more honest to do our war borrowing in the way we propose.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Lethbridge opposing our amendment because at the beginning of the war he and his party proposed total conscription: man-power, money and property. We are not by this amendment proposing conscription of money in the full sense of the term, but our proposal is a step in that direction and to that extent it should satisfy the hon. member for Lethbridge.
A great deal more could be said on this question, but I do not wish to detain the house further. I think I have proved, Mr. Speaker, that both from the point of view of sound economics and also for psychological reasons it is desirable that the government should offer compulsory non-interest-bearing loans.

Perhaps in view of what took place this afternoon in connection with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), I should say something with regard to the amendment which is now proposed.
The amendment as now proposed differs materially from the amendment which was proposed this afternoon in that the word "compulsory" has been deleted, and the position now is that an amendment has been moved that loans shall be issued without interest. If hon. members will refer to section 4 of the bill, they will find that it reads:
The governor in council may, in addition to the sums now remaining unborrowed and negotiable of the loans authorized by parliament, by any act heretofore passed, raise by way of loan, under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931-
And so on. The amendment moved applies to subsection 1 of section 4 of the bill, but proposes an alternative method of raising the money. The purpose of the bill and the purpose of the amendment are the raising of money-in the case of the bill, with interest;
War Appropriation-Ruling

in the case of the amendment, without. In Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, citation 552, it is provided:
Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, examples of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals. Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee; but these proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year. Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as, for instance, a proposal to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property as an alternative for an inhabited house duty, the necessity of new taxation, to that extent, being already declared on behalf of the crown.
In the citation which I have quoted, the pregnant words are:
. . . but these proposals must be grafted upon the financial, scheme submitted by the government. . . .
I point out to the house that the financial
scheme of the government is not now before the house. What we have is an ordinary bill for the raising of money; and in the reference at the beginning, mention is made as to the function of the committee of ways and means. This is not a committee of ways and means; it is a committee of the whole; and therefore, when exception is taken to any proposals that they must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, it is my judgment on this amendment that we are not dealing with the financial system of the government.
In May, thirteenth edition, at page 510, it is stated:
As is subsequently explained, the constitutional principle which vests in the crown the sole responsibility of incurring national expenditure, forbids an increase by the commons of a sum demanded on behalf of the crown for the service of the state. This principle, however, is apparently disregarded when the recommendation of the crown is given to a resolution empowering the expenditure of public money which, framed in general terms, places no limitation on the amount of expenditure to be authorized by the resolution. As the resolution sanctions, without any specific limitation, the application of money to be provided by parliament to certain purposes, when the clauses in a bill founded upon such a resolution are before the committee, the freedom of action sanctioned by that resolution can be exercised. The committee is not bound by the terms of the provisions which the ministers of the crown have inserted in the bill; and any member may propose to increase the grants specified in these clauses or to extend the application of the provisions of the bill, whatever may be the cost resulting therefrom, so long as the power conferred by the royal recommendation is not exceeded. Acting on this principle, when, in 1812, a committee was considering a message from the prince regent recommending, in general terms, provision to be made for the family of 
Mr. Spencer Perceval, amendments were permitted for increasing the provision proposed by the ministers. This practice has been supported by rulings from the chair, though, on the last occasion, not without remarks which deserve careful consideration.
The principle that the sanction of the crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, applies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue. No motion can therefore be made to impose a tax, save by a minister of the crown, unless such tax be in substitution, by way of equivalent, for taxation at that moment submitted to the consideration of parliament.
And, on page 512 of the same edition:
The house can make amendments which diminish the amount of a reduction of taxation, or postpone the day when the reduction takes place, although the amendments may increase to that extent the charges proposed to be levied upon the people. So long as an existing tax is not increased, iany modification of the proposed reduction may be introduced in the committee on the bill, and is regarded ias a question, not for increasing the charge upon the people, but for the determining to what extent such charge shall be reduced.
Further on, the author gives another illustration:
As a final illustration of the way in which the reduction of public charges is dealt with, it may be mentioned that, as a "drawback" is *a fiscal arrangement made to facilitate the exportation of goods liable to excise duties, and is so far an alleviation of taxation, a provision creating a "drawback" can be considered without recommendation from the crown, or a preliminary committee resolution.
While it is true that none of the illustrations given are directly apropos of the question which is now before the house, yet the principle is the same and the fact is that if the amendment carries and becomes a part of the bill, the charge against the country will be lessened rather than increased. As I have already said, this is not the financial scheme of the government, in that we are not dealing with the budget, which really embodies the financial scheme of the government. In my judgment, therefore, the amendment is in order.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the question is put, I should like to make a few observations.
The amendment now before the house differs from the amendment proposed this afternoon and also the amendments or proposals suggested previously by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group, in that it leaves out the element of compulsion. That is, nominally it leaves out the element of compulsion, lout in reality that element is present. It is quite obvious, I believe, to any hon. member who gives the matter even slight consideration that if we were to attempt to borrow $1,300,000,000, or even a small part

War Appropriation-Mr. Ilsley
of that sum, from the people of Canada without agreeing to pay interest on that loan, we would not get the money on a voluntary basis. It would be necessary to levy the loan. As a matter of fact, the word "levy" or "levied" is used in the proposed amendment. The amendment is that:
. . . under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, by way of interest-free loans to be levied according to ability to subscribe such sum or sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of one billion, three hundred million dollars as may be required for the purposes of this act.
Apparently what is proposed is the infusion into a voluntary loaning system of a compulsory loaning system, a system of forced loans. The first observation which I should like to make is that the two systems cannot exist side by side. Just as, I think, Lincoln saidi that a nation cannot exist half slave and half free, so I am sure we could not have here in Canada a system of loaning which was half compulsory and half voluntary. The effect of announcing that a substantial sum of money was going to be levied upon the people by way of forced loan would be that it would be practically useless for us to appeal for voluntary loans, because all the enthusiasm, all that spirit of democratic cooperation to which we appeal, and appeal very successfully at the present time, would dry up.
Mr. MaeINNIS: Only for raising money, but not for people to fight.

The temptation is too great and I am going to be drawn away from my line of argument just to deal with that observation. The hon. gentleman who has just interrupted has frequently said that this government is fond of conscripting men but will not conscript wealth. I heard him make an eloquent appeal on that point here last November or December. I wish to examine it for one minute. It is true that we have conscription of men in this country, but it is conscription of men to a very limited extent. If one were able to measure the extent of the conscription of men in Canada in terms of the percentage of total conscription, one would find that the conscription of human beings is far less than the percentage of conscription of wealth. Let me adduce some figures in support of that.
I believe I told the house the other day about the amount of money we are taking in taxation, which is real conscription of wealth, because there is then no obligation to repay,
as my hon. friends think there should be, apparently, to a larger extent than I think there should be.
