I can give the figures for
Saskatchewan. I have them here. They will be found in the budget speech of the then Minister of Finance on June 24, 1940, at page
War Appropriation-Mr. Ilsley

1027 of Hansard, setting out a table for all the provinces which have income taxes. To hon. gentlemen who think that we are running the government in the interests of the rich, I would recommend a perusal of that table.
What I was going to say when I was derailed by the interruption is that the blending of the two systems is impossible. We would be driven to a compulsory system. My hon. friends have been talking about inequities and injustices. The essential injustice of the compulsory system is that equity is impossible because of the differing circumstances, differing requirements and differing necessities of persons with the same income.
In so far as- equity is possible, in so far as we can determine equitably what each can pay, we determine that when we impose taxation. We impose taxation up to a pretty high level, and above that there will be some persons with a surplus who cannot, and in other instances, persons who should not, devote that surplus to the uses of the government. It might be far more advantageous to the country if they would put that surplus into capital investment and produce goods for war purposes or something of that kind, while alongside them might be another person with the same income whose surplus could not be devoted to that purpose but who should lend his money to the government. That is the reason why a voluntary system of taxation fits in equitably if there is the right spirit in the country, if the people have the right view of the matter, while the voluntary system of lending fits into the taxation system.
My hon. friends gave instances of slackers, men who got money apparently in some way or another in the war and did not show any conscience about it, who indulged in an ostentatious display in the expenditure of that money. These people are not very numerous in this dominion, and they are becoming less numerous with the growth of a proper public opinion. In England the degree to which public opinion has developed is considerable. A few weeks ago I heard Lord Kindersley on the radio, in one of the Sunday afternoon broadcasts in the interests of the war savings campaign, make the statement-I cannot remember his exact words-that public opinion had been developed to such an extent in Great Britain that the blatant spender was a social outcast. That is the state to which opinion will have to be developed in the Dominion of Canada. The compulsion is then the compulsion of public opinion, the pressure of what a man's neighbours think, what people all over the country think. That

is the system upon which we are relying, and we have been relying upon it with good results.
I do not believe I finished the thought I was attempting to develop about the impossibility of saying what one person should lend to the government and what another person should. I was dealing with the man with the big income, the man with a great deal of wealth; but when you come to people with small incomes and small amounts of wealth, and undertake to have the government say to them, "You should lend so many dollars to the government"-

There may have been some instances in which excessive pressure was exerted, but it must be remembered that in the war savings certificates drive we are not taking money away from people without interest; we are paying three per cent compound interest on the money. I should be much surprised if there were any real injustices in this connection. I think the percentage of cases in which any injustice has been done to any person, rich or poor, in this dominion, in the war savings certificates drive would be infinitesimal. On the contrary, when they have been persuaded to buy war savings certificates, in practically one hundred per cent of the cases they have been persuaded to do something greatly in their own interest as well as in the interest of the country.
As I say, I think it would be perfectly impossible for any government, by any system of compulsion or by any system of exemptions, to get substantial sums in this way with any degree of justice. We could perhaps do it up to a certain level, but if we were to get very large sums such as we get in our loan campaigns it would be impossible to say to Mr. A, "You should lend X dollars to the government," and to Mr. B, "You should lend Y dollars to the government". In one case there might be sickness in the family; there might be demands about which we would know nothing. There might be requirements, obligations a man had to meet, of which the government could have no knowledge, and for which there would be no possible way of making any allowance. That is why the ideal system is to have a healthy state of public opinion, upon which in a democracy one has to depend in order

War Appropriation-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
to get the maximum war effort. That is what we have by our system of voluntary contribution.
I am a little surprised at that group, which is so strong on freedom and liberty, rushing so quickly to compulsion in this important matter. I am always very much interested in the views expressed by both groups in the far corner opposite, and I think if we could take the best views of each group we might have a pretty good policy. For instance, I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) when he says that the creation of substantial sums of new money is a most foolish policy, particularly under present conditions. I also agreed with the leader of the social credit group this afternoon when he said a forced loan would be a bad thing under present conditions. If they would just take the best and discard the worst of the policies that emanate from that corner of the house, I think we might accept those hon. gentlemen as pretty safe guides. Unfortunately there is always a certain admixture of error with a considerable amount of truth in what they have to say.
The compulsion should, I think, be reserved for taxation for the time being. As I say, we are raising large sums by taxation. If it really were to be thought by the public of Canada that this house was to-night considering forced loans-and the government is not considering forced loans-I am afraid the results in the country to-morrow would be fairly serious. Any threat of a compulsory loan would be likely to create considerable uncertainty and fear among many people with small savings but without much understanding of financial matters. Certainly it would result in many small savings deposits being withdrawn from the banks and hoarded in the form of currency, in the hope that thereby they might be hidden and so escape any such conscription of wealth. Such action would be useless and foolish from the point of view of the individual, since in any event there is no question of confiscating bank deposits. It would mean that the owners of these small savings would lose the return on them by refusing to invest them. The well to do, on the other hand, with better sources of information, -would not be penalized by any such fears, so any fear of compulsion is apt to work damage on the poor rather than the rich. There is another type of hoarding which might result from fear of compulsory loans; that is, the hoarding of goods by those who might wish to spend their money before the government could commandeer it. This would be just as baseless a fear and as futile a reaction as the hoarding of currency, but it would be much more *contrary to the public interest. Any action of
this kind would tend to increase the scarcity of labour and materials needed for war purposes.
I think that pretty well sums up the reasons for which I would ask the house to reject this amendment. Something has been said about New Zealand. I am not familiar with the experience of that country, but I do not think they have gone very far with their proposal; at least I cannot find any evidence that they have done so. They took power to levy some compulsory loans in that country, but though I have been trying to find out what they have done I have been unable to get any information, and I doubt if the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has anything more definite than I have. I should be very much surprised if that plan really has been tried there, or, if it has been tried, if it has been a success.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take just a moment or two before this motion is put. It seems to me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) has put up an excellent straw man in order to knock him down again. In the first place the minister suggests that he is prepared to obtain money by taxation while we are suggesting that money obtained by this method should be given back; and the minister suggests that he wants to take money in much larger quantities than we are prepared to do. Of course he knows that the amendment now before the house would not in any way preclude the levying of taxes. What is suggested is that when all that can be collected out of current income is collected, the remainder must be secured from reserves. That is what we do now. The remainder must be obtained from reserves of wealth, and this motion only suggests that instead of getting that money from reserves by borrowing it at rates of interest, it shall be borrowed without interest, and that the levy shall be made on the principle of ability to pay.
In the second place I wish to point out that the minister has suggested that this government is following a policy of conscripting wealth to a much greater extent than it is conscripting men. I point out first that this conscription has been imposed upon one class to a much greater extent than upon other classes. Economic conscription has been brought to bear upon thousands of men in Canada, particularly unemployed young men and those in the distressed areas of this country, many of whom have flocked into the fighting services not only for patriotic reasons but also because of economic motives. What has the minister to substantiate his claim
1S62	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
that wealth is making its contribution? He quotes some figures which in themselves are fantastic. When the minister talks about incomes of $500,000, he knows very well that last year there were only 483 people in Canada who received incomes of $50,000 to $100,000 and up. That statement is contained in an answer given on March 17 by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) to a question asked by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw). So those people in the $500,000 income bracket, about whom the minister spoke, are simply non-existent.
The important matter, however, is not to read to this house or the country figures showing how much a man pays when he has an income of $100,000. I note just one or two of the figures. I notice, for instance, that, according to the minister, a man in Ontario with an income of $100,000 has to pay $56,000. That is not the important thing. The important thing is that he has $44,000 left. Does the minister suggest that any man who has an income of $44,000 a year, when this country is at war, is making the greatest possible contribution he could make to the winning of this war? At this time we ought not to ask what a man pays in taxes when he has $44,000 a year left to spend. That man does not know anything about conscription of wealth, or anything else.
The amendment now before the house asks for the introduction of two principles: First, that over and above taxes the money which the government must secure from reserves other than current income shall be levied on the basis of ability to pay. We are levying on reserves now; that is why we float loans. In the main they do not come out of current income. Taxes come out of current income, but loans come out of reserves or savings. Voluntary loans, however, are made on the basis that the person with the greatest sense of public duty subscribes. We collect our loans now from the people who have the greatest sense of public duty; and we entirely overlook, and allow to slack-and I use the minister's own expression-that person who has no sense of public duty.
The outstanding principle included in this amendment is that for the first time we shall begin to tax those reserves on the basis of the ability to contribute toward the winning of this war. The second principle is that we shall eliminate the payment of interest, because by the time this war is over, the major part of the bonds having been contributed to a very large extent by a minority of the people, we shall find that we shall have mortgaged Canada for a generation or two to come, and that at the present rate at the end of four years we shall have sold bonds which

will be equivalent in value to practically all the farm land in Canada. We shall find that we, our children and our children's children will continue to pay interest to those very people who are now in a position out of their reserves of wealth, apart from their incomes, to subscribe to the government's war effort. We are suggesting that the people who have reserves of wealth shall contribute on the basis of ability to pay, but having in mind that generations after us shall pay back contributions made without having to pay toll and tribute year after year, as we did after the last war.
I should like to close with this observation: The minister has said that if this policy were announced to-night it would cause fear from one end of Canada to the other. I tell the minister I believe it would cause confidence in many parts of Canada. It would cause many of our people to feel for the first time that we are really all in the front line, and that this government is now calling upon every Canadian citizen on the basis of his ability to contribute toward the financing of the war. It would give to the men in the fighting services and to those people across Canada who pay innumerable taxes and are already carrying a great load, a feeling that for the first time the government is calling upon those who have the ability to pay, to shoulder their fair share of the burden of carrying on this war.

speechtext:
War Appropriation-Mr. Quelch
tvhy do we not obtain the money from our own bank, the Bank of Canada, instead of from the chartered banks, who will merely create the means of payment?
That is when the minister interjected that it would be inflationary. This is the reason the minister gave for saying that it would be inflationary. He stated that when money is issued by the Bank of Canada, that money eventually finds its way into the cash reserves of the chartered banks; that is to say, the cash reserves of the chartered banks will be increased by that amount. In view of the fact that they are operating on a ten to one basis; they would then be able to expand their loans hv ten times the amount of the increased cash reserves. This is exactly the same reason which Mr Dunning gave on previous occasions. What does this really mean? It means that we dare not use the Bank of Canada for fear the chartered banks will expand their loans and thereby bring about inflation. In other words, it proves conclusively that up to date this government has not established effective control over the issue of credit by the chartered banks. Yet time and again we have been told in this house that we have. The former Minister of Finance, Mr. Dunning, told us that we had absolute and effective control over the chartered banks. I should like to quote what the former Minister of Finance said in this regard on February 28, 1938. He said:
Parliament through instruments which it has created and which are now in operation does control currency and credit in Canada day by day, week by week and month by month.
And yet we dare not issue money through the Bank of Canada for fear the chartered banks will expand their credit. As I say, this shows conclusively that we have not obtained effective control over the issue of credit by the chartered banks. Is it not strange that we should have a national bank and yet not be in a position to use it because we are afraid of the action the chartered banks may take? Surely the first thing to be done, something which ought to have been done long ago, is to establish effective control over the chartered banks. When I spoke on March 20, I outlined three methods by which that control might be effected. I suggested the 100 per cent money system advocated by many leading economists and bankers. I pointed out also that it would not be necessary to go that far, that one could merely increase the cash reserve requirements of the chartered banks to an extent where they would not be able to utilize the new issue of cash for the purpose of expanding their loans. I suggested also that we might buy the shares of the chartered banks.
I maintain that any one of these three methods would give us control of the chartered banks so that we could issue money through the Bank of Canada without any danger whatsoever of the chartered banks increasing their loans. Until we do that, we shall never be in a position to finance the expenditures of this country without debt. That is my main objection, really the only objection I have to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. It would increase our debt, and I consider that in war time we ought to adopt a really pay-as-you-go policy. No one should desire or hope to benefit materially as a result of the war. I should like to read a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on August 2, 1935. He said:
Until the control of the issue of currency and credit-
Very often the word "credit" is left out.
-is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile. To regain for the nation what has been lost and to secure a properly constituted national central bank will continue to be a first objective of Liberal effort.
Will anyone dare to suggest for one moment that this objective has been reached when we dare not issue money through the Bank of Canada without fear of the chartered banks creating inflation by expanding loans to ten times the amount of the cash issued by the Bank of Canada? That seems to me to be a rather unfortunate position for this government or this country to find itself in at the present time.

speechtext:
Yes; but that is saying that we will control credit by removing the basis for credit. That is a negative stand to take. I quote further from the remarks of the Prime Minister as to why this bank was to be established:
It stands for the immediate establishment of a properly constituted national central bank, to perform the functions of rediscount, and the control of currency issued, considered in terms of public need. A central bank is necessary to determine the supply of currency in relation to the domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people.
I do not think anyone can maintain that during the past five years credit and currency have been made available in terms of public need, to meet the domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people. When we had during that period a million

War Appropriation-Division
people on relief, a half million people unemployed, can anyone say that currency and credit were made available to meet the social requirements of the Canadian people? I should like to give the house the definition of inflation which was given by a former minister of finance to show that credit could have been issued safely at that time without danger of inflation. The hon. member for Lethbridge said this:
The minute you get more money in circulation, let me repeat, than enough to do the work of distributing goods and services which are abroad in a country to be distributed, then you have inflation, and not a minute before.
The then Minister of Finance, Mr. Dunning, said that he agreed. No one will suggest that there was enough money in circulation from 1935 to 1939 to exchange the goods and services available at that time. The minister admitted himself in 1939 that it was necessary to have a degree of carefully controlled monetary expansion in order quickly to put people to work, in order quickly to bring industry to full production. The same thing could have been done from 1935 to 1939. Yet every time that we urged the government to issue money through the Bank of Canada we were given the same excuse the minister gave on March 20, that we cannot do it for fear the chartered banks would create inflation by expanding their credit on the basis of the cash issued. This proves conclusively that we have not established effective control over credit. I remember that in the past the Minister of Finance said, when we suggested that $200,000,000 should be issued to build up a national works programme, that the issue of $200,000,000 would not in itself cause inflation; but when the chartered banks acquired that $200,000,000, he said, and expanded it to $2,000,000,000, he was old-fashioned enough to think that would cause inflation. But, Mr. Speaker, if any of the three proposals I have mentioned were adopted, it would be impossible for the chartered banks to expand their loans on that basis.
Now that this subject has again come up for discussion, I wonder whether the Minister of Finance could not give us a better excuse -perhaps I should say reason, but I think I am justified in using the word "excuse"- than the one he gave us the other day, that we cannot use the Bank of Canada because the chartered banks are likely to expand their credit on the basis of the cash issued through the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1941
speechtext:
This resolution precedes
the introduction of a bill providing for the renewal of the agreement between the federal government and the city of Ottawa by which
[Mr. Speaker.)
the federal government pays to the city the sum of $100,000 as compensation for water used for sprinkling purposes in parks and also for fire protection.
A number of years ago, as hon. members will recall, the city of Ottawa made a claim against the federal government on the ground that a number of properties had been taken over by the government, thus depriving the city of the taxes previously imposed upon these private properties. Several points of discussion were raised, but finally, after negotiation, an agreement was reached, I believe, about the year 1920. By that agreement the city was to be paid $75,000 a year for the services to which I have referred. A few years afterwards the agreement was extended for a period of five years on the understanding that the $75,000 would be increased to $100,000 a year. That agreement was in force up to the year 1930. Since 1930 it has been extended every year by a bill similar to the one which will be introduced if this resolution carries.
I do not know that I can add very much more by way of explanation. This is an old procedure which has been followed every year. Some people might suggest that it was about time we made an agreement which would last for more than one year, but that would reopen all the questions which were raised when the first agreement was negotiated, and certainly for this year, in the difficult times through which we are passing, I do not think it would be opportune to reopen the matter with a view to reaching a new agreement.
The criticism has been made that we are not giving similar compensation or payment to other cities. My reply is that Ottawa is in a peculiar position because the federal government controls a much larger number of properties in this city than in any other city in the dominion; and these properties being exempt from taxation, the city of Ottawa is exposed to the loss of a much larger amount of taxes than any other city in the country.
Judging from the favourable reception given to similar proposals in years gone by, I sincerely hope that the committee will support the resolution and allow the bill to be introduced.

speechtext:
The principle under which this grant is made originated some years ago, at a meeting of the municipalities of Canada. At that time it was pointed out that in Australia each province gave a cash grant to the capital city in exchange for municipal services. For example, the government of New South Wales helps to maintain the police and fire departments of the city of Sydney. I do not desire to oppose this grant to the city of Ottawa; far from it. But when you add this amount of $100,000 to the amount spent by the Ottawa improvement commission and the other large sums of money spent in this city-I think there was a year ago something like $8,000,000 for new buildings-it amounts to a very large sum. This $100,000 and the amount spent on other Ottawa parks work are equivalent to about two and a quarter mills in the Ottawa tax rate, and to that extent this government is lessening the taxes which otherwise would have to be paid by the people of this city.
The principle underlying this grant should be applied to the provincial capitals as well. It applies in the United States, where they give what is known as a subvention to the capital in exchange for certain civic services to the state such as police protection, fire protection, water, health regulation, street cleaning and so on.
That is the situation in times of peace, but this is a time of war, and the war has placed a very heavy burden on the municipalities. In the first place, the government comes along and appropriates their revenues. The income tax was the exclusive field of the municipalities from 1867 to 1917. That field has been taken over by the provinces and invaded by the dominion, and now hon. gentlemen opposite are threatening what they are going to do in the way of appropriating more of municipal and other provincial revenues. The result will be that our municipalities will starve, because all their money must come from taxes on real estate and they can get no help anywhere.
That is not a fair condition. Every vote must have a principle, and if the principle of
City oj Ottawa Agreement

this vote is sound, then I believe it should apply to the larger municipalities throughout the country. The city of Toronto, for instance, gets little or nothing no matter what government is in power. Why, Toronto has to pay the cost of guarding the hydroelectric power plants and other city property, and the distribution system covering the whole of Toronto, which furnishes all the power used by the munitions factories of that great city. We do not get a cent for that. During the last war the federal government paid the cost of guarding, by the militia in training, all federal, provincial and municipal property, but that is not so to-day. The province of Ontario came to Ottawa with regard to that matter, and this government last fall receded from its position and took over the cost of guarding the power plants in the Niagara district, but did nothing about the distribution power system of the municipalities; it let them pay for that work.
In my view this principle should be applied to other municipalities in addition to Ottawa. Some contribution should be made by this government in exchange for the services rendered as well by the larger municipalities. In Toronto the government has been given the use of the exhibition buildings and grounds, which cost $24,000,000 of the taxpayers' money on grounds, buildings and permanent exhibits. Those buildings and grounds were used for military purposes in the last war, and are similarly used in this one, and this government does not pay a cent for them. It does not even pay the cost of lighting the grounds.
This government has thus placed a very heavy burden upon the municipalities. Almost every statute passed by this parliament adds to that burden, but the municipalities are not given a dollar in subventions. That is inequitable and unfair. Here Ottawa is given a grant amounting to about two and a quarter mills in the tax rate, while the other municipalities can get nothing at all. Here we are voting about three billion dollars, presumably for war purposes, although a great deal of it is not for the war at all. It must be remembered that some war work is also being done by the municipalities, and they pay part of the federal burdens. Toronto has, in its tax rate, about two mills of purely federal burden.
Since I have been in this house I have urged that the government should heed the handwriting on the wall. I believe the principle under which this grant is made originated when I was president of the union of Canadian municipalities. We adopted a motion urging that the government should give subventions to the larger centres of population in exchange for municipal services, but so far that

principle has been extended only to the city of Ottawa. I believe some recognition should be granted the other cities that give a great deal more in the way of the services than is given by the city of Ottawa. I urge the minister to consider this point. Two years ago he said he would do so, but he has not considered it at all. In view of the heavy burden of taxation municipalities are paying, a contribution of two or three mills to the tax rate would look particularly good, especially in view of the fact that the government is taking large revenue from municipalities. We seem to have the principle of the law of the jungle-"to him that hath shall be given, and to him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath." I see no reason why the city of Ottawa should not have some recognition; but I must say, as I said last year when a similar bill was under consideration, that some consideration might be given to other cities in this connection.
It was pointed out by me last year that there is not sufficient room for all the war departments of the government, and I suggested that many of them should be moved to Toronto, Hamilton, Montreal and other points where housing and building space are available. I believe such a movement would effect great economies. When the minister replied, he said the matter would be taken up, but it has not been.
Where is the government going to get space? I suggest that great economies could be effected by a rearrangement of departments and their transfer to other cities and towns. I hope the minister will give us some explanation of this expenditure. Why is it that there is always discrimination against the city of Toronto? No matter what government is in office, we receive the same treatment. We contribute tax moneys to the extent of nearly $92,000,000, and we get nothing in return but pin-money. I say we are entitled to recognition. We have no post office. We had a new mail order building, but it was taken away and given to the military authorities for an ordnance department. Toronto paid one-third of the cost of the viaduct, a sum it had no right to pay, at all. It has contributed large sums of money to the federal exchequer; it is behind the government, and wants to help it. I hope, however, that after the representations I have made, the minister will give the matter some consideration. I believe that in other places they do receive better treatment. I hope other members of the Conservative party from Ontario will take a similar stand. I

City of Ottawa Agreement
would hope, too, that members on the government side might do likewise. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Gibson) a minister, is in his seat to-night, and I hope he will take that stand. I shall not plead their cases for them, but I do say they are entitled to just as much money as is the city of Ottawa. I should like to know the views of the hon. member for Hamilton West regarding this policy of treating cities in a different manner, because he is a member of the government.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER

speechtext: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 14, to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act (fish and shellfish).

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill which deals with the canning and care of lobsters. It appears suitable for that purpose. Since I have only a limited knowledge of that matter, I shall leave it to hon. members from the maritimes to deal with the question in detail. There is, however, one small matter I should like to call to the attention of the minister. Perhaps he will

Meat and Canned Foods Act-Fish
be kind enough to look into this and change the bill when it is in committee. The old act required certain facts to be placed upon the label of each can, among them being the name of the place where the article was packed. That applied, not to salmon, but only to shellfish, but through some rearrangement of the wording of the section, quite inadvertently I am sure, it has been made to apply to fish salmon, or herrings and pilchards.
This brings in the salmon trade of British Columbia. It is required that this information be placed upon the labels of each can. Salmon is put up in one pound, half-pound, and, I believe, quarter-pound tins, and this will mean a lot of work. What is required to be put on the label is the place where it was packed, not where it came from, and that gives no information at all. Supposing a housewife buys a can of salmon and she wants to purchase another similar can; if the label simply states that it was packed in a place called Ivildonan, it gives no information as to where the salmon really came from.
Of late years there has grown up a system of transporting salmon from the place where it is caught to a central point. In the old days it was packed in the cannery at the place, involving large expenditures for hauling supplies back and forth and people, also houses, schools, doctors and so forth. But better transportation methods have allowed it to be done the reverse way, and now the tendency is to bring the salmon to where the centres are and where the population ensures that the cannery can easily get a supply of labour at a few moments' notice. The consequence is that while the fish might be regarded as being packed in Vancouver, it might have been caught a couple of hundred miles away. That gives a wrong impression as to the point of origin. These big companies in British Columbia often have a number of canneries, and some of the fish may be caught in one place and some at another place, and a precise statement of where they are packed is asked for.
The proposed method is inconvenient, expensive and unjust. Every intelligent citizen of British Columbia knows that fish of any variety are always caught in their best excellence in the district I have the honour to represent, and that applies to other things than fish. A fish might be caught at Kildonan or at Barkley sound or some other place on the west coast and be transported to Vancouver to be packed. It would be regarded as packed in Vancouver. But the same identical fish might be packed next week or next month at Kildonan. Also, of course, the history of a particular catch would have
to be carried out in its entirety, can by can. You might have 26,000 cases of sockeye sold to Britain, some of them packed in one place and some in another, and the same with any of the other main, known and acknowledged varieties-sockeye, springs, chums, and so on. The inspection of salmon in British Columbia is scientifically carried out, and when that test is passed and the stamp is put on certifying that the fish is No. 1 sockeye, or whatever the variety may be, from British Columbia, the public in Britain can be perfectly sure that they are getting a first-class article, no matter where it was packed.
What is really required is that, instead of putting on the name of the place where the fish is packed, the name of the province should be put on. That is the usual custom of the trade, and it is better for the customer as well as for the purchaser. Then the British housewife buying a tin of No. 1 sockeye can tell whether it was packed in British Columbia, but if she -asks about a particular cannery, they would not be able to tell her where it came from. The suggestion I make would be to the distinct advantage of the business and of the packers, and I do not think it would detract in any way from the object which the minister has in mind in bringing in this amendment. I hope he will agree to make it the name of the province.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I entirely agree with the suggestions that have been made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. The purpose of this amendment is to enable the department to make regulations along the lines my hon. friend suggests, particularly with regard to canned lobster. If the amendment passes, it will enable the department to make rules and regulations to correct not only the anomalies pointed out by the hon. member with regard to canned lobster but anomalies with respect to other kinds of shellfish as well as salmon. That is exactly the purpose for which this amendment to the Meat and Canned Foods Act is sought.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to section 1 of this bill, which gives a new definition. In the old act we referred to lobster as lobster meat. It takes quite a stretch of the imagination to call any fish meat. You would have a comprehensive definition of the word "meat" to label a can of lobster as "lobster meat."
I think the elimination of the words "dry lobster meat," in the present act is a most commendable change. The bill in its entirety is for the purpose of ensuring proper super-

Meat and Canned Foods Act-Fish
vision and inspection of the sale of lobster both in Canada and for export, and as such deserves the support of the house.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Vien in the chair.
On section 1-"Dry meat."

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext:

kinds of packed lobster meat-dry meat and meat that is not dry-or is it all dry meat?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext:
There is only one kind of lobster meat put into cans, and the trade description of that lobster meat is "dry meat." The purpose of the amendment is to eliminate the detailed description, "dry lobster meat," and to substitute the words "dry meat." I am told that the former detailed description was necessitated by the provisions of section 23, which is repealed by this amendment and a new section substituted therefor. The words . "dry lobster meat" will no longer be necessary. To avoid misunderstanding on the part of packers, dealers and sometimes brokers, it has been decided that it would be better to eliminate those words.
Since this bill was printed, it has been found that the definition of "dry meat" contained in clause 1 is a little ambiguous, and it is proposed to clarify it, without changing the meaning at all. I would ask my colleague to move an amendment accordingly. The new definition will read:
"Dry meat" means the meat of shellfish contained in a can which has been processed and allowed to cool thoroughly, and which is opened and upturned for not less than one minute and not more than one and one-half minutes so as to permit free drainage of the liquor therefrom.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER

The only change is that, for the reasons I have mentioned, I have put in the word "province" instead of the word "place." I believe this would be much more convenient to the cannery people and to the whole industry, as well as to the buying public, and would better carry out the purpose of the original act.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext: I am satisfied to agree with what the hon. member has suggested, although I believe it will not make much difference, because the phrase, "the name of the place where the same was packed" is inclusive enough to cover the name of the locality and the province where the pack is put up. In my opinion, even though we have these words in the act, they will enable us to make regulations providing for placing on the can the name of the place, as in some circumstances may be required, particularly for lobster; and in the case of salmon it would not prevent us from making regulations provided that it is sufficient to have the name of the province on the can. With regard to the lobster there are packs put up in certain districts of the maritime provinces where the locality gives some trade value to the goods, and we want to be sure we have power to provide that the name of the place where the goods are put up is indicated on the can. I feel that the existing wording is broad enough to enable us also to make regulations covering the case of canned salmon, where the name of the province would be sufficient.

speechtext:
The section carries out that idea in part, but it goes on to say, "in the case of fish." "Fish," I take it, means, other than shellfish.

weight . . .

I would say, with no offence at all to the minister-for I do not care who the minister is; the idea is the same-that I do not care for the idea of accepting assurances in this house that such-and-so put into an act is going to mean something other than it exactly does read, and of trusting that later on it will be so carried out. I well recall, in connection with a bill dealing with soldier settlement, pointing out an anomaly somewhat similar to this one, and saying that I was afraid that

Meat and Canned Foods Act-Fish
it might be interpreted later on by officials in a manner prejudicial to the settler. The minister in charge-he is no longer here^-said that I could accept his assurance in the presence of the whole house that it would not be so interpreted. Six months later I had occasion to protest against the treatment of a settler under the strict wording of the act, and I was told by the officials that they had nothing to do with the statement made in the house by the minister, that it did not bind them and that they did not propose to be bound; and in consequence of that, the settler suffered a grievance. The minister expressly stated in the presence of the house and the whole government that the interpretation would be such-and-so. That happened on more than one occasion, and that is why I am a little dubious about accepting the assertion that everything will be lovely.
I quite admit that to put all this pedigree that the act calls for, about the lobster, is perhaps necessary. It always has been so, and I am not seeking to make it different. I am only seeking to preserve the purity, so to speak, of the British Columbia salmon as regards the province it comes from, .without going into any ridiculous demand which might involve putting the exact spot where it was packed. In days gone by there used to be floating canneries where the packing was done wherever the boat happened to be. You would have to take the degrees of latitude and longitude every night in order to ascertain exactly where the boat might be at the moment certain packing was going on, and when a canner is putting up 50,000 cases every year, with six or seven varieties, he cannot keep track of every half or quarter-pound tin, or a lengthy pedigree of the source and origin and where the fish in each tin was packed; it would be a heavy expense, and expense at any time means poor business, because the product would cost more to the consumer and yield less to the fisherman. I will not press the amendment, because the government has a large majority behind it; I am merely putting in my protest. Expense and inconvenience will be caused, with no benefit to anybody at all.

There is a slight change
in order to make this section clear. I will ask my colleague to move the amendment, which is as follows:
That section 4 be struck out and the following substituted in lieu thereof:
4.	Subsection two of section twenty-two of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
(2) Any unsound fish or shellfish found during the process of preparing and packing, and any unsound canned fish or shellfish found at any time thereafter, as provided by the regulations, may be seized and confiscated on view by any inspecting officer and dealt with as required by the regulations.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext: Might it not be possible for unsound fish or shellfish to be found prior to preparing and packing. The inspectors, in the course of their rounds, might find unsound fish prior to preparing and packing, so I think it should read, "found at any time before or thereafter".

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext: The section now provides for the confiscation of unsound fish or shellfish found during the process of preparing and packing. The whole process starts with the bringing of the fish to the cannery or place of packing. Then it is prepared for packing and placed in the can. This provides for seizing the fish at any time, from the moment they are taken into the cannery until they are put into the cans. Then follow the words, "and any unsound canned fish or shellfish found thereafter," which means after it has been prepared and put in the cans. The cans are sealed; then on second or third inspection they may be found to be unsound, and this provides for their seizure as well.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext: The section reads, "any unsound canned fish". That would mean the fish would be in the can.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext: What is the purpose of this change?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION AND MARKETING PROVISIONS TO CANNED LOBSTER
speechtext: As it stands now, the regulations are statutory. The canned lobster trade is changing rapidly; we have to find new markets in the United States for a large part of the pack, and we find it necessary to make regulations different from those that existed in the past. We must meet the conditions with which we are faced when we market our lobsters, so instead of having the regulations statutory, we are taking power to make the regulations by order in council.

Section agreed to.
